Alloy 454 is a single-crystal nickel superalloy used for advanced jet engine turbine blades and vanes.
The gamma-prime (γ') phase content in both Alloy 454 and the reference alloy Mar-M 247 was around 60%.
The 0.2% yield strength and tensile strength of Alloy 454 increased gradually up to 700-800°C, then decreased at higher temperatures.
The creep rupture strength of Alloy 454 was greater than the reference alloys like Mar-M 247, particularly at temperatures over 900°C.
At 760°C, Alloy 454 showed much stronger anisotropy in tensile and creep properties compared to other nickel superalloys.
Orientations near the -111 and 011 axes in Alloy 454 exhibited only 3/4 the strength of the 001 orientation at 760°C.
The -111 orientation in Alloy 454 showed remarkably low strength, nearly equal to the 001 orientation, in contrast to other alloys.
TEM analysis showed severe deformation and roughening of the gamma-prime phase in the -111 oriented sample, with concentrated {100}<110> slip in the gamma phase.
The Schmid factor analysis indicated that the typically favorable {111}<112> slip system had a relatively low Schmid factor in Alloy 454 near the -111 orientation.
The high strength of the gamma-prime phase in Alloy 454 forced the activation of less favorable slip systems like {100}<110>, leading to the observed anisotropy.
Solution treatment at higher temperatures and the high tantalum content in Alloy 454 contributed to its improved creep rupture strength at elevated temperatures.
The anisotropy in Alloy 454 was attributed to the available slip systems and the stacking geometry of the gamma-prime precipitates.
Alloy 454 showed little change in strength within 20 degrees off-axis from the 001 orientation, in contrast to other alloys.
The rupture surface morphology of the samples also reflected the differences in the dominant deformation mechanisms.
The single-crystal nature of Alloy 454 allowed for optimization of the vane performance by tailoring the crystal alignment.
